blocks.x: Let me see, this is Real One of Emil Barnes. Tell everybody your full name now, huh?
My full name is Emil Barnes.
Your full name is Emil Barnes?
Emil Barnes. Some call me middle, short name, you know. But I'm well known by Emil Barnes.

And what's your name? Herb Friedwald. Well, my name is Dick Allen and let's see, we're recording today at 3610 Metropolitan Street. It's January the 3rd, 1962. Okay, Herbie, you want to ask me something?

Well, I wanted to ask Emil about some of the clarinet players that you don't hear too much about now that he knows. The different ones that played with Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly and those guys way back. Not the clarinet players that would be known as reading musicians, but some of the other ones.

Well, I'll tell you something about that. The clarinet players that played with, well, I remember Lil Pills. That was the only name I knew anymore. Now they had another one that was the clarinet players that was the clarinet players that was the clarinet players. Now, the clarinet players that was from the lower coast. Then again, between time, they had another one there by the name of, let's see now what they call him. Charlie, Charlie, Charlie. Well, he was a pretty good clarinet player. That's about all I could remember of this time and mention that clarinet. Well, how would you describe the way they played, Mealy? Well, they were pretty fair. It wasn't out to call them musicians because they weren't much a breeder like myself. But at the meantime, they could take the place of pretty much any musicians. They were really good players. Would you say they had good ears? They could pick up tunes well? Oh, yes. You couldn't get away from them in no kind of way. It ain't because there was so much in them that what they couldn't get to, they'd violate them. With the old clarinet, the old clarinet players, they'd violate them. But I know what they call it now, but it makes something a little different.
Like a variation. Yeah. Now, who were they again? Let's see now, Zeb?
That was Zeb and Pills and Charlie. See, that's what Blind Charlie's called.
Blind Charlie. Well, how did these fellows look, Mealy? Would you describe them?

Well, Charlie was always near-sighted. Pills was a little short fellow, kind of yullish, yullish, you know, but he was crippled. He was crippled. And Zeb was a tall fellow, him, very slow in talking. He didn't talk much in that time. What part of town did they come from? Well, Zeb and Pills both was from the low coast. Yeah, that, what I would call it, Verrett, you see? That Verrett village. In other words, well, you see, Charlie was from here. He was from Mount Gravity Street. He was from Mount Gravity Street. Yeah, he was from Mount Gravity Street at that time.
What about Pills' brother, Ninny Quacko? You remember Ninny?

Yeah, Ninny Quacko. Well, Ninny Quacko was, uh, was alright, but, uh, he didn't bother much with us. You see? It was a guy mistaken. The Ninny went off, and Ninny Quacko went off here with a shoe. Mm-hmm. That's years ago. And, uh, you know, we never heard, uh, once, I believe we heard from him once. That's it all.
He's out in California last year, and I believe he's alive out in Los Angeles.
Well, I'm surprised that one would read it. I wouldn't know him now if he'd walk upon me. He wouldn't know me.
Did he look like Pills?

Well, he was a heavier, heavier man in Pills. You know, he was much heavier than Pills. But they were all pretty much the same color. Did he play variety, Ninny? Well, Ninny was playing alright, but the trouble to see, he was more like a musician playing, you know? See, he didn't make nothing but this direct stuff. But, uh, you wouldn't say Pills was like that? No, Pills was the man that threw a swing any way that you swung.
Uh, what about this other clarinet player that, uh, we never heard, this, uh, Georgia Boy?
Oh, Georgia Boy, he's a man who went with Pudgy all the time. He was a pretty good clarinet player, too, Georgia Boy.
Did he play on the order of Pills and Zeb and those fellas? Well, yeah. He played on that order, too.

He played on all of them. He was a big sport. He gathered himself away, in other words, because he was well-knowing and well-liking. So, George, I was sorry. See him, he wasn't in TB. He wasn't in TB and we lost him.
Did he have a rougher tone or was he smoother or what?

Well, them fellas, uh, pretty much had more of a higher tone. They never would, uh, go, uh, uh, carnage, uh, eating staff or below or nothing. They, they always was, uh, playing high, high tonic, you know? Yeah.
Did they take solos where they would be the only horn playing? Did they do any of that, Mealy?

Well, I'mma tell you about that right now, horn. For us solos, I never heard solos in my life until, uh, as late to him. Because the only solos that we have when we play all, uh, two that had clarinet parts in it. That was the only solo. Oh, I see. Special parts like, uh. Yeah. Special, that's direct for them clarinet or chime on or call that, you see. But if this would take a solo, we didn't do that. Only solo that we would take, well, we wouldn't call it solo. We'd call it a, uh, a lead. That's in order for a chime on or a trumpet or all the rest to dry their lips.
Then we'd call it another part and they'd come in and allow for it. I see. So, you wouldn't necessarily, uh, take the lead in the same place in the same tune every time you played it.

No, sir. I never known of that. That's just right to him. And it would just come up. Yeah. I never heard of that before, but, uh, that, that's really a new style, which I believe, I'm sure, that any old musician will tell you that.

Well, I can't pretty much remember the tune now, but such as Grace and Brody and Grace and Beauty and, uh, and, uh, Black and White, and, uh, well, it's different numbers. Uh-huh.

Well, you hold it, you sit on it, take a rest day, you move on. By the time I come back in, that's the way I'll figure it out. But for instance, a solo now, I don't know, it's different. Uh-huh. Yeah, pretty much all of them in the ground is different. It's hard to get a, uh, a real Dixieland man who's out there for us to find out, you catch some of the first men, such as, uh, Peter Bugga, or, well, that's about the only man here that I can remember just now leading. But anyhow, some of the old-time men, real old-time men are the second-class men as myself. Yeah. Cause see, Peter, I put them before me. Yeah. And I'm second one, the rest is off.
Uh-huh. Yeah. Well, now, I mean, back in the old days when you would play, take the lead, would the people applaud after you finished taking the clarinet part alone like you do now?
Oh, man, man, yeah.
Yeah, they'd applaud for individual things like that.

Uh-huh. Well, they applaud for it at that time, but at the meantime, when the tune was empty, when the tune was through, they'd stop and they'd stop and they'd clap and clap and tell you, you had to play it over, they wouldn't stop. But for us to have taken a solo and they'd clap? No. No.
No. But at the end of the number?

At the end of the number, if a person like the tune of a bunch on the floor would like that to- They'd like to hold to them. They'd stand up and they'd clap, they'd stomp, they'd holler, they'd do everything, to get that number going over again. After it gets going over, well, it's all right, they'd be satisfied.
I see.

Some numbers, yeah.
Not just a solo, but a part. You had certain, that's the bass part, the drum part, and the clarinet part, just like that.
Would the bass ever have the lead?

Well, with some numbers, the kids. Let's see. Well, I couldn't too well get the number right today, but I know the bass had a lead in it. Yeah, I couldn't get it so right today, but bass would just bow down. Not pitch, bow. He would bow down to a certain part, and the band would take it. He would play melody on the bass? That's right, melody, lead like a violin.
Well, I want to ask you about another tune that there's a special clarinet part now that a lot of the old timers play at the St. Louis Blues. Oh, well yeah, that's a special. That's a special.

No. No, it didn't come from the orchestra, because we played it, we just liked it, that part in it, so the band would leave a clarinet mate there. So that's a special chorus, isn't it? Yeah, a special chorus. Whose chorus is it? No, I mean, is there any clarinet player that taught it up, any one guy? Where did you first hear it?
Well, I don't know, over the way I got it at, but I'll tell you the truth.

Years ago, a long time ago, we couldn't play nothing but that for the boys. Like we had our boy here at Simon J. Peterson's school up there, and we know the band could play by the table at school. You see, on a certain reason, just on that part, they thought it was so fine, they gritted, and men of them were liking it.
It's a special chorus. I know George Lewis plays it, Piku played it, Burbank played it. I believe Big R. Louis. Well you told me once, Mealy, or am I wrong, that you heard it from Big R. Louis.

Well I did. I did got it from Big R. Louis, and if I'm mistaken, I think Big R. Louis, he come up with it. If I'm mistaken, I'm because I really caught in my mind now, it's a lemon. I don't know, they don't play the outside of him. You take, for instance, George Braquet. You take, how do you call them that, Piku, none of them didn't make it. Oh, they didn't play it then?
Didn't play it then, no.

Later years.

Later years. But the force would come now. Now you see, I learned from Piku, George. But my ideas were from Lloyd. Now Big R. Louis was a man that played a clarinet. And he could take a clarinet and make a rooster, curl, dog bark, anything like that. And that's why I learned he told him that problem. Right on the end, because if he was playing the hill, I wouldn't dance or go out there. I wouldn't have to hang him or nothing from him.
Would you say he was your favorite of all the ones you heard?
Oh yes. Who was your favorite? The favorites over all the musicians. Over the musicians.
He never did any of that freak stuff in late years. I wonder why.

Well I don't know. I couldn't tell you why or how. But Louis, for his part, he was always a more clarinet player than any of them. Now why did I say that? You take for instance that the Millen Boy, Spanish food. We take for instance the Millen Boy first. If Louis was playing here, and Rocky and Piku and all them around, you could hear different tones and the different things he'd make. It was more valuable to me. I wouldn't say about you, and what any of those other folks. It was more valuable to me. Yeah.
He had more originality then.
Yes. That's what I think about it.
Well, did he mostly read music when he played? No. Louis wasn't a reader.

Louis was a speller. He wasn't a good reader? No. He was speller. Piku, George, and all of them was readers. But Louis wasn't? Louis was. Louis would spell a whole lot. He couldn't really make a full line. He couldn't take a piece of music up and go down with it. He'd take a piece of music, look at it, run over it, and then he'd go down with it.
Who would you say would play with more feelings? Bike and Piku or Big Arui? Bike. Bike.
Bike. Bike.
Oh.

playing it was tough. Was Louis fast? Fast, yeah. Fast all the way through. Did you like his tone? His tone was great. That's why I picked the tone of the movie. Did he play a lot of low register or mostly high register?

Well not for me.

Say you were playing with him and he got pretty far off the melody. What would you do on clarinet then?
The clarinet would pick lower and down. I see.

No, man, because the most of these men, cabaret, cabaret men and band men, men played a lot in politics.

segments.title: Opening of reel one, names and recording location
segments.summary: Dick Allen and Herb Friedwald introduce themselves and Emil Barnes, giving the address and the date, January 3, 1962.

segments.title: Lil Pills, Zeb and Blind Charlie: the lesser-known clarinetists
segments.summary: Barnes recalls the clarinetists who played with Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly, how they played, and what they looked like and where they came from.

segments.title: Pills's brother Ninny Quacko
segments.summary: Barnes describes Ninny, who left town long ago, and compares his playing and build with Pills's.

segments.title: Georgia Boy and the high tone of the old clarinetists
segments.summary: Georgia Boy, who went with Pudgy, is remembered as a good player lost young; the clarinetists played high.

segments.title: Solos, leads and applause in the old days
segments.summary: Barnes explains there were no solos as such, only special parts or leads to rest other horns' lips, and audiences clapped at the end of a number, not for solos.

segments.title: Special clarinet parts on High Society and bass parts
segments.summary: How the clarinet played the High Society part with trumpet seconding it, and how bass and drum had parts rather than solos, including bowed melody.

segments.title: The special clarinet chorus on St. Louis Blues
segments.summary: Barnes says the clarinet chorus did not come from the orchestra; the band simply liked it and left it for the clarinet.

segments.title: Big Eye Louis as favorite clarinetist: tone, originality, reading
segments.summary: Barnes says he got the chorus from Big Eye Louis and ranks him over Piku and others for tone and originality; Louis was a speller rather than a reader.

segments.title: Rough and growling clarinet: Lorenzo Tio
segments.summary: Asked who played rough, Barnes names the younger Tio with his heavy reed, whom he says could get rough though he sounds smooth on records.

segments.title: How clarinetists played off the melody, Keppard
segments.summary: Clarinet and trumpet kept partly the same melody; when a man like Freddie Keppard strayed, the clarinet picked lower and took the melody over.

segments.chapter: Blues, cabarets and the Golden Room
segments.title: Who played blues before records; holes in the wall and Storyville
segments.summary: Barnes names Bechet, Dodds, Blind Charlie and Kaiser as blues men in small bands in district cabarets, with no cutting contests, and mentions the clarinetists and trumpeters of the time.

segments.chapter: Blues, cabarets and the Golden Room
segments.title: Blind Charlie's blues playing
segments.summary: Barnes says Charlie worked in tonks and cabarets with a short man and played more melody; Barnes struggles to describe his blues.

segments.chapter: Blues, cabarets and the Golden Room
segments.title: The band at the Golden Room with cousin Mitchell Frazier
segments.summary: Barnes names his cousin Frazier and the Golden Room band; the talk turns to the quiet neighborhood around it.

segments.chapter: Blues, cabarets and the Golden Room
segments.title: Blues then and now, playing the blues all night
segments.summary: Barnes says the blues were different in the old days and recalls playing blues from eight until three or four.

segments.title: Kimball and the Robichaux band; blues with introductions
segments.summary: Reel two opens on Kimball, a reader who could play blues, probably in Robichaux's band, and on old blues played with an introduction.

segments.title: What makes a real old-time band: violin lead, old numbers
segments.summary: Barnes says he would like to hear a real old-time band, with violin leading and old tunes such as Maple Leaf, instead of newer open-key numbers.

segments.title: Robbing the music: Big Eye Louis and Bunk versus Robichaux's readers
segments.summary: Non-readers like Big Eye Louis and Bunk rearranged note values by feel, whereas Robichaux's orchestra played what was written; Barnes prefers small bands.

segments.title: Whipping Johnny Dodds with Bechet at St. Catherine Hall
segments.summary: Barnes and Bechet used to out-play Dodds, who was then with Oliver at St. Catherine Hall, and Barnes says Bechet was a pal.

segments.title: Who read music: Dodds, Charlie, Jimmie Noone
segments.summary: Barnes compares the reading ability of Bechet, Dodds, Blind Charlie and Noone, called Jimbo, and how loud and rough each was.

segments.title: Fast fingering: Tio, Jimbo, Bigard and Nicholas
segments.summary: Barnes says Tio and others were fast, Jimbo about the same, and that Bigard and Nicholas became fast only after going north.

segments.title: Clarinetists in town in the 1920s: Humphrey, Lewis, Handy, Burbank
segments.summary: Barnes recalls whether Willie Humphrey, George Lewis, John Handy and Albert Burbank were around and respected in the 1920s.

segments.title: Cottrell, Chris Kelly, Kaiser, McCurtis and the Morgans
segments.summary: Barnes discusses Louis Cottrell with Kelly, Kelly's temper, and other clarinetists including Kaiser, Charlie McCurtis, Joe Watkins and Andrew Morgan.

segments.title: When the saxophone arrived in New Orleans
segments.summary: Barnes says clarinetists like Kaiser did not play saxophone, and the saxophone came to the city late, with Big Eye Louis bringing one back.

segments.title: Blind Charlie's tonk bands and piano players
segments.summary: Barnes says Charlie played in small tonk groups, with the Martins and Coochie as pianists and guitarists.

segments.title: Kaiser's brass band work and clarinetists with Kid Ory's band
segments.summary: Kaiser played brass bands and orchestras; Barnes recalls who was in Ory's band, and says men swapped clarinetists freely.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden's Funky Butt
segments.summary: Dick Allen asks how Funky Butt went; Barnes cannot recall it.

segments.chapter: Blind Charlie, kin and early memories
segments.title: Where Blind Charlie is now, and his missing last name
segments.summary: The group tries to identify Blind Charlie, whom Barnes met a year ago, and Barnes explains musicians are known by first names only.

segments.chapter: Blind Charlie, kin and early memories
segments.title: Uncle Tartone and the Marrero and Frazier cousins
segments.summary: Barnes lists musical relatives: his uncle, the Marrero cousins, the Fraziers, Dave Williams and an aunt who played guitar.

segments.chapter: Blind Charlie, kin and early memories
segments.title: Birthplace and the surprise-party bands
segments.summary: Barnes gives where he was born, then explains the serenade-style surprise party bands of violin, bass, guitar and clarinet, with no trombones.

segments.title: Reel three opening; Bunk Johnson at the Eagle Hall and the first clarinet
segments.summary: Barnes says no one in his family played, and he first got a clarinet through Bunk after the Eagle Band at Eagle Hall.

segments.title: Playing the flute and piccolo; the tune 'Got good booty'
segments.summary: Barnes first played a small flute on his own and learned one tune, which he describes.

segments.title: First band: the Ambrose Power job down the river
segments.summary: Barnes's first real job was a four-piece band with Ambrose, Henry Ford and others, playing all night at a dance down the river.

segments.title: Ninth Ward musicians and crossing the river for jobs
segments.summary: Barnes names musicians from downriver and the Ninth Ward, including a valve trombonist, guitar players and Joe Hoodoo, and mentions crossing to jobs.

segments.title: Learning numbers and jobs with the little band; picnics and Gettysburg March
segments.summary: Barnes describes the violin lead, learning tunes by ear and playing picnics up to about age nineteen.

segments.title: Playing with Clem: the band, style and tonguing
segments.summary: Barnes joins Clem's band, whose leader he compares to Kid Thomas, and the group discusses tonguing in trumpet playing.

segments.title: Working several bands at once; Joe Howard and the 1915 storm
segments.summary: Barnes was in a regular band with Clem while also working for Joe Howard and others, around the time of the 1915 storm.

segments.title: Playing with Chris Kelly and the Johnny Brown band
segments.summary: Barnes talks about joining Kelly's band, its changing personnel, Johnny Brown's earlier band, and playing with Kelly before and after the Depression.

segments.title: Kelly's band during World War I: Marrero, Bond and drummers
segments.summary: Barnes recalls Kelly's personnel in the First World War, including Lawrence Marrero on banjo and various drummers, and says he worked with many bands.

segments.title: The best drummers: Dave Benny and Facer
segments.summary: Barnes praises Dave Benny, who danced with his drums, and Facer as the best drummers he sat next to.

segments.title: Working with Bunk; the Imperial and Superior bands
segments.summary: Barnes worked with Bunk after Bunk got him his clarinet, lists men in Bunk's band, and the group sorts out the Imperial and Superior bands and Jimmie Noone.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Where Barnes lived and the Young Imperial band
segments.summary: Barnes tries to place his addresses and recalls the Imperial Band with his cousins, a drummer and a trumpeter.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Playing with Kid Thomas across the river
segments.summary: Barnes explains how Thomas hired him after hearing him in Kelly's band, how Paul also joined, and Thomas's costumes and work.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Leading his own band at Raceland and Grand Island
segments.summary: After Thomas, Barnes ran a band for a dance hall owner near Raceland, at times fourteen pieces and two jobs, in the 1930s.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Playing with Buddy Petit; no early records
segments.summary: Barnes played often with Petit and Kelly but recalls no recordings before his late ones.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: How he came to record, and the Home Inn
segments.summary: Two collectors asked him to record while he worked at the Home Inn; he describes building up a small club.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Dick Allen's first visit to New Orleans and hearing Barnes
segments.summary: Allen tells of a weekend when he caught three bands, including Barnes's, and Friedwald recalls seeing Paul Barnes.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Other neighborhood clubs: River Bell, Mama Lou's, Lodgett's, Manny's
segments.summary: Barnes lists the clubs he worked after the Home Inn, with Lawrence on trumpet, and playing trombone at Manny's.

segments.chapter: Thomas, own bands and neighborhood clubs
segments.title: Lenny Dawson and other bass players
segments.summary: Barnes praises his longtime bass player and mentions the band at another club.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, union and theatre work
segments.title: Brass band work and the union
segments.summary: Barnes says he played most brass bands but fell away after quarrelling over union dues.

segments.chapter: Brass bands, union and theatre work
segments.title: The theatre band at the Palace under Howard
segments.summary: Barnes played show tunes by ear in the Palace theatre band led by trumpeter Howard, with Paul in the group.

segments.title: Every clarinetist once had his own sound
segments.summary: Barnes says he wants to sound only like himself, and that today's players sound more alike.

segments.title: Tunk brass bands and how brotherhood has changed
segments.summary: Barnes describes ear brass bands playing dance music in the streets, and how clubs have made musicians less friendly than when Steve died.

segments.title: Will the old style come back?
segments.summary: Barnes believes the old men could easily revive it but the young will not, and he dislikes today's music.

segments.title: End of the interview
segments.summary: Allen closes the tape and thanks Barnes.
